name: Beth Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for this, Beth. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Whatever you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a pole replacement crew for the power company, working the river valley. Wooden poles rot at the ground line after forty or fifty years, so we test them, dig out the bad ones and set new ones beside them, then move the wires across. Some weeks we're on right-of-way instead, clearing the trees under the lines with saws. I came up through a four-year apprenticeship and I'm proud of that.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm married to Daniel, who runs his grandfather's hardware store on Bridge Street. We live in the flat above it, and we own a share of the business, so between that and what I've saved we're secure. On Saturdays I help in the shop, and on Sundays it's church and lunch with his parents. I also look out for our apprentice, Jonah, he's nineteen and reminds me of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, these things always get oversold. People at church were worried about it, so I'd tell them they can relax. I don't post online much, just the church newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my life carries on as planned. Poles rot, we replace them, that's forty years of work in this valley alone. I'd be glad, because I like my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new. Keep working, keep saving, and Daniel and I would start trying for a family next year like we planned. Maybe put a bit more into the store.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI for anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. Daniel and I used it to sort out the store's stock ordering, which was a mess of paper. And I sometimes ask it to tidy up the church newsletter. I check everything, though, it gets things wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would this mean for Jonah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd have a good long career, like I'm hoping to. That's what an apprenticeship is for. In this picture, nobody has to worry about that.

S0.say: She'd say she isn't surprised, since such things are always oversold, and tell worried people at church they can relax. Her only online writing is the church newsletter.
S0.think: She thinks her life carries on as planned, with forty years of rotting poles to replace in her valley alone. She'd be glad, because she likes her life.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving, and starts trying for a family next year with her husband as planned. Might put a little more money into the hardware store.
S0.quote: Poles rot, we replace them, that's forty years of work in this valley alone.
S0.fieldNote: Beth's life is settled and clearly mapped: work, the family store, church and plans for children. She uses AI occasionally and practically, for stock ordering and the newsletter, and checks its output. Her apprenticeship and her mentoring of Jonah are central to how she sees herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is part of life, and the answer is training, proper apprenticeships for whatever new jobs come. I wouldn't be complaining about it. I'd say businesses should train their people, not just let them go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job's safe in this one. The boring office bits might change, the forms and the planning. Digging out a rotten pole by a river bank still needs people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever new tools the company brought in, once I'd seen them work on another crew first. I'd keep helping Jonah along and make sure he learns the new bits too. Otherwise, same plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could change on a pole replacement crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Testing the poles, perhaps. Right now we tap them with a hammer and drill a little hole to check the wood. A machine that could tell you from a scan would save time. I'd welcome that, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the store be affected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little, if online shops get cleverer. But people come to Daniel because he knows which screw you need and he'll talk to you for twenty minutes. That's not something you can copy easily.

S1.say: She'd say change is part of life and the answer is proper apprenticeships for new jobs, with businesses training their people rather than letting them go. She wouldn't complain.
S1.think: She thinks her job is safe here: forms and planning might change, but digging out a rotten pole on a river bank still needs people.
S1.do: Learns new company tools once she's seen them work on another crew. Keeps mentoring Jonah, making sure he learns the new methods too, and otherwise sticks to her plans.
S1.quote: Digging out a rotten pole by a river bank still needs people.
S1.fieldNote: She wants businesses rather than government to carry the burden of retraining, in the form of apprenticeships. She'd welcome a scanning tool for pole testing, which shows her openness once something is proven. Her husband's store feels safe to her because of personal service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say this is where families and communities show what they're made of. I'd say businesses owe it to their workers to give notice and train them for whatever's left. I wouldn't be calling for handouts, but I'd want employers to step up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is frightening. If robots can set poles, I'm out by twenty-nine. I'd have the store to fall back on, which is a blessing, but it's Daniel's family business, not my trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put everything I could into savings straight away and cut out the extras, the new car we'd been looking at, the holiday. I'd talk to Daniel about starting a tool hire and repair counter at the store, something I could run with my hands. And I'd keep my job right up to the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd pray about it a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned starting a family next year. Does that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think we'd still try. Children come when they come, and I wouldn't want a robot deciding that for us. We'd be more careful with money, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the store really a safe place to land, if robots reach everywhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not completely, no. Nothing is, in that picture. But people in the valley will still want to talk to a person when their roof leaks, I think. Maybe I'm hoping more than knowing.

S2.say: She'd say this is when families and communities show what they're made of, and that businesses owe workers notice and training. She wouldn't call for handouts, but wants employers to step up.
S2.think: She finds two years frightening: if robots can set poles, she's out of work by twenty-nine. The store is a blessing to fall back on, but it's her husband's family business, not her trade.
S2.do: Moves everything she can into savings, drops the planned new car and holiday, and proposes a tool hire and repair counter at the store that she could run. Keeps her job to the end and still plans to start a family.
S2.feel: Anxious, and praying about it a lot.
S2.quote: Children come when they come, and I wouldn't want a robot deciding that for us.
S2.fieldNote: Faith and family plans hold steady even in the fastest picture; she refuses to let it change her plans for children. She is honest that the store is her husband's business and that its safety is partly hope. Her ideas for the store use her hands-on skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to prepare, so we should. Apprenticeships for new kinds of work, businesses planning ahead, people looking after each other. That's what I'd say at church and at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough to build up the store with Daniel so it can carry both of us. I'd be thirty-two, maybe with a little one. It feels possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the tool hire and repair counter properly in the first year, and put some of our savings into it. I'd use AI for the ordering and the bookings, since we already do a bit. Then I'd drop to part-time on the crew in a couple of years and move over gradually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but hopeful. There's time to do things right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the years before 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is grab what you can and hold on. Five years is build something properly. I like building things properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Jonah in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to finish his apprenticeship, because it'll teach him to work, and then learn whatever the robots need. Someone will have to fix them. I'd want the company to give him that chance.

S3.say: She'd say there's time to prepare, with apprenticeships for new work, businesses planning ahead and people looking after each other. She'd say it at church and at work.
S3.think: She thinks five years is enough to grow the store with her husband until it can support both of them. At thirty-two, perhaps with a child, it feels possible.
S3.do: Opens the tool hire and repair counter properly in the first year, investing some savings, and uses AI for ordering and bookings. Drops to part-time on the crew after a couple of years and moves over gradually.
S3.feel: Uneasy but hopeful, because there's time to do things right.
S3.quote: Two years is grab what you can and hold on. Five years is build something properly.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her plan a gradual move from the crew to the family store, timed and financed. She sees a human role in fixing robots and wants the company to give the apprentice that chance. Her language about doing things properly ties to her apprenticeship pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing, plenty of time for people to plan and train. I'd tell the younger ones to take an apprenticeship and learn to fix things, robots included. I'd be quite upbeat about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think we'd be fine. The store would be bigger, I'd have years more savings, and I'd probably have moved over by then anyway. God has never left our family without work to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working on the crew for most of it, help Daniel grow the store and add the repair counter in a few years. I'd keep saving and putting money into the business. No rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Grateful for the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a danger of feeling too relaxed with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. People always think they've got more time than they do. But I'd have the store as a reminder every Saturday, so I don't think I'd forget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it comes, what would you want the company to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep its apprentices on and teach them to look after the machines. And tell us clearly when it's coming, so we can plan. That's not much to ask.

S4.say: She'd say a decade is a blessing, with plenty of time to plan and train, and tell young people to take apprenticeships and learn to fix things, robots included. She'd be upbeat.
S4.think: She thinks they'd be fine, with a bigger store, years more savings and probably a move to the store already made. She trusts that God has never left her family without work.
S4.do: Stays on the crew for most of the decade, helps grow the store and adds the repair counter in a few years. Keeps saving and investing in the business without rushing.
S4.feel: Calm and grateful for the time.
S4.quote: God has never left our family without work to do.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Beth is calm, resting on faith, the family store and a long runway. She accepts the risk of complacency but expects her Saturdays at the store to keep her focused. Her asks of the employer stay modest: keep apprentices, train them for the machines and give clear notice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's the only one where I'd have to grab and hold on instead of building something properly. What would help is employers giving real notice and keeping apprentices on to learn the new machines, and the community looking after its own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith. A lot of people at our church are scared of this. I think a community that meets every week is better placed than most to get through it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Thank you. That's everything I needed.

headlineQuote: I think a community that meets every week is better placed than most to get through it.
portrait: Beth Haddad is a 27-year-old lineworker on a pole replacement and tree-clearing crew in a river valley, who came up through a four-year apprenticeship and now mentors a nineteen-year-old apprentice. She is married to Daniel, lives above his family's hardware store, owns a share of it and uses AI now and then for stock ordering and the church newsletter. She is calm through the milder pictures, expecting rotten poles to need replacing for decades. A two-year AGI warning makes her anxious, but she would save, cut extras and still try for a baby, while five or ten years lead her to build a repair counter at the store and move over gradually. Faith, family and apprenticeships shape all her answers.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she would have to grab and hold on instead of building something properly.
whatWouldHelp: Employers giving real notice and keeping apprentices on to learn the new machines, with the community looking after its own.
